title: Photons and hydrogen energy levels
promptMarkdown:
Use $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 2.998\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $R_H = 2.179\times10^{-18}\ \text{J}$ (the constant OpenStax 6.2 calls $k$), $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Treat the hydrogen atom with $E_n = -R_H/n^2$.

1. Compute the wavelength, in nm, of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron drops from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$, and say which region of the spectrum it lies in.
2. Compute the ionisation energy of ground-state hydrogen in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
3. Can a photon of wavelength $400$ nm ionise a ground-state hydrogen atom? Give its energy in J and in eV and decide.
4. The same $400$ nm light falls on a metal surface whose work function is stated to be $2.30$ eV (a value given for this exercise, not a property to look up). Compute the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons in eV. Then say what happens to that kinetic energy if the light intensity is doubled at the same wavelength, and why.
hintLadder: The photon energy is the difference of two level energies: $\Delta E = R_H\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)$ for $n_i \to n_f$. Then $\lambda = hc/\Delta E$.
Ionising ground-state hydrogen takes the electron from $n = 1$ to $n = \infty$; multiply the per-atom energy by $N_A$ and convert joules to kilojoules.
Compare the 400 nm photon's energy with $R_H$; a photon either has enough energy or it does not.
In the photoelectric relation $\text{KE}_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$, which quantity does intensity change? Count photons, not energy per photon.

checkExamples.label: correct answer
checkExamples.text: ΔE = 2.179e-18 (1/4 − 1/9) = 3.026e-19 J, so λ = hc/ΔE = 1.986e-25/3.026e-19 = 6.564e-7 m = 656.4 nm, red visible light. IE = 2.179e-18 J × 6.022e23 = 1.312e6 J/mol = 1312 kJ/mol. A 400 nm photon has E = 4.966e-19 J = 3.10 eV, far below 13.6 eV, so it cannot ionise ground-state hydrogen. KE_max = 3.10 − 2.30 = 0.80 eV. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and hence of electrons; the kinetic energy of each stays 0.80 eV because it depends only on frequency.

checkExamples.label: wrong transition and classical intensity reasoning
checkExamples.text: The 3 → 2 line is at 486 nm. Doubling the intensity doubles the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons because more energy arrives per second.
